# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## Traditional Toughness and Its Flaws

When college students described toughness, words like hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, and persevering came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked first. The traditional view equates toughness with overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, and stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man. This model ties toughness to masculinity and machismo: we tell sons and daughters to “man up” or “stop being a pussy,” and romanticize the Karate Kid narrative of getting bullied then coming back with vengeance. The language reveals a confusion of toughness with callousness—hardening, making insensitive, developing thick skin. We rationalize absurdity in youth sports: parents justify making eleven-year-olds go until they puke as necessary “to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.” The old model is a remnant of military-style drill sergeants and coaches who thought like them.

## The Bobby Knight Model

Bobby Knight won over 900 games, three NCAA championships, and coached the undefeated 1976 Indiana team. He defined toughness as “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His methods included tampons hung in lockers of players he thought “soft,” frequent cussing, a 1991 tirade (“This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground…”), bringing toilet paper with feces to show players what he thought of them, and choking a player on video. Knight’s actual definition: showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, using fear to establish authority and control. This version—now called “old-school” to distance from barbaric practices—still dominates playing fields and performance halls.

## Authoritarian Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind classified parenting styles by two factors: responsiveness (attunement to children’s needs) and demandingness (expectations and control). Authoritarian parents are high in demandingness, low in responsiveness—relying on fear, threats, and punishment. A typical refrain: “You need to do (this) because I said so.” In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. The ideal is authoritative parenting—high in both demandingness and responsiveness—which fosters independence and self-regulation. Punishment and expectations are not bad per se; the problem is extreme mismatch between demand and support. The same principles apply to coaching and leading: we’ve taken the demanding part and forgotten warmth, care, and responsiveness.

## Consequences of Callous Toughness

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed signs of profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches yelled to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” It took 34 minutes to remove him from the field, another 28 minutes to call 911—1 hour 28 minutes total before the ambulance arrived. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, has become common from extreme workouts designed to “test” athletes, not improve fitness. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, these workouts aim to “toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse. In sport, it’s linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In one study of 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse with military challenges. One young athlete explained: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger… I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.” The old model creates fragile, dependent individuals who respond only to external fear. As the swimming analogy suggests, throwing every kid into the deep end works for some but proves disastrous for many.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.” It’s about providing the tool set to handle adversity—teaching, not bulldozing. The military, often seen as the epitome of demanding toughness, has actually been perfecting this other model of resilience for decades.

Pete Carroll, one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl, believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, and bouncing back. He told The Bleacher Report: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do.” Other successful coaches using humanistic approaches include Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni, who told the author, “We keep it positive here.” As Ken Reed summarized, “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach.”

In 2008, Eastern Washington University researchers studied nearly 200 basketball players and concluded: “The ‘keys’ to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

## The Author’s Personal Story

The author collapsed during a Don Bowden Mile race at Cal, experiencing a high-pitched gasp and inability to breathe. After a year of tests—scopes down his throat, echocardiograms, treadmill and biking tests to exhaustion—allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD). The vocal cords, controlled by reflex, shut when they should open, triggered by strong emotions and stress. The American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress as triggers. The author’s strategy of pushing until he puked backfired, exacerbating the issue. To race again, he had to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the moment of peak discomfort. This search for real toughness led to the book’s four pillars: Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; Listen to Your Body; Respond Instead of React; Transcend Discomfort. As podcaster Rich Roll summarized, “Everybody goes through shit in their life. Nobody escapes obstacles.”

# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## Basic Categories & Hard Edges

Seven primary types: Projects list, project support material, calendar actions/information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, reference material, Someday/Maybe list. Categories must be kept pristinely distinct—each represents a discrete type of agreement with yourself. If reference mixes with reading, you go numb to the stack. If calendar items stay on action lists, you won’t trust your calendar. Projects not being acted on go on Someday/Maybe so Projects list retains action-generating focus. Waiting For mixed with action lists causes nonproductive rethinking.

## Lists and Folders

Lists track projects, someday/maybes, actions. Folders hold reference and project support. Don’t impose external priority scaffolding requiring rearrangement—you’ll prioritize intuitively against shifting variables. A "list" can be: (1) file folder with separate paper notes, (2) titled paper in loose-leaf organizer, or (3) inventory in software or mobile device.

## Organizing Action Reminders

After processing "in," you'll have pending items plus delegated reminders and calendar/someday items. Sort into meaningful groupings.

### Calendar Actions

Two kinds: time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") and day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Calendar should show only the "hard landscape"—exact hard edges of your day's commitments. Resist putting actions you'd like to do but might not; they belong in "as soon as possible" categories.

### As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context

Best reminded by context: tool, location, or situation needed. How discrete categories need to be depends on (1) how many actions you track and (2) how often you change contexts. With 25 next actions, a single list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting. Leveraging energy in a mode (phone mode, computer mode) is supported.

#### Common Categories

- **Calls** – all phone calls needed. Record phone numbers alongside each item.
- **At Computer** – actions requiring a computer. Author maintains separate "Online" list for when Wi-Fi is unavailable (e.g., on planes).
- **Errands** – things to do when out. Sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with appended items). Location-based reminders are emerging but overoptimistic for total trust.
- **At Office** – actions requiring physical presence (e.g., purging filing cabinet). "Hotel-ing" (no permanent office) is rising; may need multiple At Office lists.
- **At Home** – e.g., "Hang new watercolor print," "Organize travel accessories," "Switch closets to winter clothes." If you work only at home, At Home suffices.
- **Agendas** – items to cover with someone or in a meeting. Separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, financial advisers, etc. Standing meetings (staff, board, committee) deserve their own lists. Add ad hoc as needed.
- **Read/Review** – longer-than-two-minute reading items. Best managed in separate physical stack tray labeled "Read/Review." Some professionals (e.g., attorneys) may also need "Review/Respond" category. Digital: "Review/Watch" file or "Surf Web" action list.

### Organizing "Waiting For"

Reminders of things you're waiting for from others (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, OK on proposal). Not action steps but triggers. Review as needed to check status. Keep close to Next Actions lists; responsibility may bounce back and forth. Include date requested and agreed-upon due date—"But I placed the order March twentieth" is worth its weight in gold.

### Original Item as Action Reminder

Exceptions: Read/Review articles (magazine in tray), paper bills in "Bills to Pay" folder, receipts in "Receipts to Process" envelope. Danger: if not reviewed consistently, just organizing isn't enough. Reminders should be in visibly discrete categories based on next action required—not all documents of one type sorted together despite different actions needed.

For e-mail: create @ACTION folder (prefix with @ or - to sort at top) for longer-than-two-minute actionable e-mails. Create @WAITING FOR folder for delegated items (cc/bcc yourself). Getting e-mail "in" to empty means deleting, filing reference, doing <2-min responses, moving actionable and waiting items to folders. @ACTION is an extension of At Computer list.

#### Caution About Dispersing Reminders

Distributing action triggers across folders, lists, and e-mail is OK only if you review all categories equally. Digital data offscreen can disappear as a prompt; this has caused many to revert to paper planners for physical trust.

## Organizing Project Reminders

Create one Projects list in simple format (digital category, loose-leaf page, or file folder). It's a comprehensive index of open loops, not a priority-ordered plan. You can't do a project; you can only do action steps. Real value lies in complete weekly review ensuring action steps defined for all projects.

### Value of Complete Projects List

- Critical for control and focus – "I've got to get my driver's license renewed" can take as much headspace as "I need to formulate the agenda for next year's conference."
- Alleviates subtle tensions – small things morph into bigger ones (e.g., preschool registration problems, invoice disputes).
- Core of the Weekly Review – linchpin for marrying larger commitments to day-to-day.
- Facilitates relationship management – enables negotiation of explicit and implicit agreements with bosses, staff, partners.

### Where to Look for Hidden Projects

1. **Current activities** – calendar meetings, action lists, workspaces (e.g., conference call about client request → "Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ").
2. **Higher-horizon interests** – professional goals, company objectives, strategic plans, personal life (kids aging, retirement, partner's aspirations).
3. **Current problems, issues, opportunities** – problems (always projects), process improvements, creative/capacity-building opportunities. Examples: "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance," "Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner."

### One List or Subdivided?

Most find one list best as master inventory. Common subsorts: Personal/Professional (personal list needs weekday review too), Delegated Projects (for senior managers), Specific Types (e.g., "Projects—Presentations" chronological list for speakers, sales relationships in progress). How you group is less critical than completeness and regular review.

### Subprojects

If moving into a new residence, subprojects like "Finalize the patio," "Upgrade the kitchen," "Set up home office space" could be separate entries or held as support material. Author's example: "Move to Amsterdam" was one project, then unpacked into fifteen (from "Set up Dutch bank accounts" to "Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara"). Recommend putting big projects on Projects list and subpieces in support material, reviewed weekly.

## Project Support Materials

Resources to support actions and thinking, not reminders. Don't use support material for reminding—that creates mental noise. First add project to Projects list, put action steps on appropriate lists, then pull materials when doing actions. For example, "Upgrades—37 Pinkerton Place" folder with plans; during Weekly Review, pull file, check for missing next actions, then refile.

### Organizing Ad Hoc Project Thinking

Options: attached notes to list items (digital or Post-it), e-mail reference folders (e.g., "Johnson Partnership—Active" and "Johnson Partnership—Archive"), paper-based files, loose-leaf notebook pages. Key: consistently look for action steps in notes and review as needed. Clear out stale notes.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

Three categories: reference materials, someday/maybes, trash.

### Reference Materials

Once actionable vs. nonactionable is cleanly distinguished, reference has no pull—it's just your library. General-reference filing (1–4 physical drawers, dozens of e-mail folders). Large-category filing (50+ folders → own section/drawer/database). Contact managers are pure reference—don't use them for action reminders. Libraries/archives: decide what needs to be with you always, in briefcase, in office, archived, or findable on Web.

### Someday/Maybes

Track things to reassess later. Examples: "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage." Author learned flute and sailing from this list. Sources: creative imagination (hobbies, skills, trips, toys) and reassessing current projects (move optional projects here). Subcategorize if helpful (e.g., "parking lot" vs. "bucket list").

Special categories: Food (recipes, restaurants, wines), Children (things to do), Books to read, Music to download, Movies to see, Gift ideas, Web sites, Weekend trips, Ideas—Misc.

Avoid "Hold and Review" files—people hold but don't review. After processing, often nothing left.

#### Using Calendar for Future Options

Three uses: triggers for activating projects (e.g., product launches, budget reviews, birthdays), events to participate in (seminars, conferences), decision catalysts (hire/fire, merge/acquire, change job/career). "It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system."

#### Tickler File

43 folders: 31 daily (1–31) and 12 monthly. Daily files in front starting with tomorrow's date; monthly files behind. Each day, empty that day's folder into in-tray, refile at back. Perpetual file. Allows storing actual documents (forms, agendas, invoices). Must check daily.

## Checklists: Creative and Reminders

Checklists are "recipes of potential ingredients" for projects, processes, events, areas of responsibility. Alfred North Whitehead: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Atul Gawande's *The Checklist Manifesto* is referenced.

First identify inherent projects and actions from fuzzy commitments (e.g., "Exercise more regularly" → "Set up regular exercise program" + "Call Sally for suggestion about gyms"). For things like "Maintain good morale on my team," create a project with action step.

Blueprint key areas of work and accountability: career goals, service, family, relationships, community, health/energy, financial resources, creative expression. Within job: team morale, processes, timelines, staff issues, workload, communications, technology.

The more novel the situation, the more control required. If CEO disappears and you fill in, you need overview outlines. Author created checklists for accounting, computers, marketing, legal, administration when taking on new responsibilities.

Checklists at all levels: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. Be ready to create and eliminate as needed.
